List I: (a) Benevolent (b) Meticulous (c) Ephemeral (d) Gregarious
List II: (i) lasting a very short time (ii) fond of the company of others (iii) kind and generous (iv) very careful about detail
questions.solution: Benevolent = kind and generous (iii); meticulous = very careful about detail (iv); ephemeral = lasting a very short time (i); gregarious = fond of company (ii).

questions.question: If A = 2134 and B = 10−12, then AB equals:
questions.solution: Row × column: (1,1) = 2·1 + 1·(−1) = 1; (1,2) = 2·0 + 1·2 = 2; (2,1) = 3·1 + 4·(−1) = −1; (2,2) = 3·0 + 4·2 = 8. (The second option is BA, which is different because matrix multiplication is not commutative. The third multiplies entry by entry, and the fourth adds the matrices.)

questions.question: If A is a 3 × 3 skew-symmetric matrix, the sum of its diagonal entries is:
questions.solution: In a skew-symmetric matrix Aᵀ = −A, so every diagonal entry satisfies aᵢᵢ = −aᵢᵢ, i.e. aᵢᵢ = 0. The sum is 0 whatever the other entries are.

questions.question: The inverse of A = 2312 is:
questions.solution: |A| = 2·2 − 3·1 = 1. For a 2 × 2 matrix, A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) × (swap the diagonal entries and change the sign of the other two), which gives the first option. Check: A·A⁻¹ = I.

questions.question: The value of the determinant 123045106 is:
Using determinants, what is the area of the triangle with vertices (1, 0), (6, 0) and (4, 3)?
questions.solution: Area = ½ |det| of the rows (x, y, 1): ½ |1(0 − 3) − 0 + 1(18 − 0)| = ½ × 15 = 7.5. (Check: base 5 on the x-axis, height 3 gives ½ × 5 × 3 = 7.5.)

questions.question: If y = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1, what is the value of d²y/dx² at x = 1?
questions.solution: dy/dx = 3x² − 12x + 9 and d²y/dx² = 6x − 12. At x = 1 this is −6. (0 is the value of dy/dx at x = 1.)

questions.question: The function f(x) = x³ − 3x is strictly decreasing on the interval:
questions.solution: f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 3(x − 1)(x + 1), which is negative exactly when −1 < x < 1. On (1, ∞) and (−∞, −1), f is increasing.

questions.question: What is the maximum value of f(x) = −x² + 4x + 5?
questions.solution: f′(x) = −2x + 4 = 0 gives x = 2, and f″(x) = −2 < 0, so x = 2 is a maximum. f(2) = −4 + 8 + 5 = 9.

questions.question: Evaluate ∫₀¹ x eˣ dx.
questions.solution: By parts with u = x, dv = eˣ dx: ∫ x eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ. From 0 to 1: (e − e) − (0 − 1) = 1.

questions.question: ∫ dx / (x² + 9) equals:
questions.solution: Use the standard result ∫ dx/(x² + a²) = (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + C with a = 3.

questions.question: Evaluate ∫₀^{π/2} sin²x dx.
questions.solution: sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2. Integrating from 0 to π/2 gives [x/2 − sin 2x/4] = π/4 − 0 = π/4.

questions.question: What is the area of the region bounded by the curve y = x², the x-axis and the lines x = 0 and x = 3?
questions.solution: Area = ∫₀³ x² dx = [x³/3] from 0 to 3 = 27/3 = 9.

questions.question: What are the order and the degree of the differential equation (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx)⁴ + y = 0?
questions.solution: The order is that of the highest derivative present, d²y/dx², so it is 2. The degree is the power of that highest-order derivative (the equation is a polynomial in the derivatives), which is 3.

questions.question: If dy/dx = y/x and y = 2 when x = 1, what is y when x = 3?
questions.solution: Separate variables: dy/y = dx/x, so log|y| = log|x| + c and y = kx. y(1) = 2 gives k = 2, so y = 2x and y(3) = 6.

questions.question: Two fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers is 8?
questions.solution: Out of 36 equally likely outcomes, a sum of 8 comes from (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3) and (6,2): 5 outcomes. P = 5/36.

questions.question: Maximise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x ≤ 3, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. The maximum value of Z is:
questions.solution: The corner points of the feasible region are (0, 0), (3, 0), (3, 1) and (0, 4). Z = 0, 9, 11 and 8 there, so the maximum is 11, at (3, 1). (12 would need x = 4, which breaks x ≤ 3.)

questions.question: On the set {1, 2, 3}, the relation R = {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2), (2, 1)} is:
questions.solution: Reflexive: (1,1), (2,2) and (3,3) are all present. Symmetric: (1,2) and (2,1) are both present. Transitive: every chain is closed, e.g. (1,2) and (2,1) give (1,1), which is in R. So R is an equivalence relation, with classes {1, 2} and {3}.
options: reflexive and symmetric, but not transitive

questions.question: How many one-one functions are there from A = {1, 2, 3} to B = {a, b, c, d}?
questions.solution: 1 can go to any of 4 elements, 2 to any of the remaining 3, and 3 to any of the remaining 2: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. (64 = 4³ counts all functions.)

questions.question: What is the principal value of sin⁻¹(−1/2)?
questions.solution: The principal range of sin⁻¹ is [−π/2, π/2]. sin(−π/6) = −1/2, and −π/6 lies in that range. (sin 7π/6 is also −1/2, but 7π/6 is outside the principal range.)

questions.question: f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2, and f(2) = k. For which value of k is f continuous at x = 2?
questions.solution: For x ≠ 2, f(x) = (x − 2)(x + 2)/(x − 2) = x + 2, which tends to 4 as x → 2. Continuity needs f(2) = 4, so k = 4.

questions.question: If y = e²ˣ sin x, then dy/dx at x = 0 is:
questions.solution: Product rule: dy/dx = 2e²ˣ sin x + e²ˣ cos x. At x = 0: 0 + 1·1 = 1.

questions.question: The radius of a circle is increasing at 2 cm/s. How fast is its area increasing when the radius is 5 cm?
questions.solution: A = πr², so dA/dt = 2πr · dr/dt = 2π × 5 × 2 = 20π cm²/s.

questions.question: What is the area of the parallelogram whose adjacent sides are a = î + 2ĵ and b = 3î + k̂?
What is the angle between two lines whose direction ratios are 1, 1, 0 and 0, 1, 1?
questions.solution: cos θ = |a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂| / (√(a₁² + b₁² + c₁²) √(a₂² + b₂² + c₂²)) = (0 + 1 + 0)/(√2 · √2) = 1/2, so θ = 60°.

questions.question: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Which statement is true?
questions.solution: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5, which equals P(A). Also P(A)P(B) = 0.2 = P(A ∩ B), so A and B are independent. They are not mutually exclusive, since P(A ∩ B) ≠ 0.
options: P(A | B) = 0.5, and A and B are independent
P(A | B) = 0.4, and A and B are independent
P(A | B) = 0.5, and A and B are not independent
P(A | B) = 0.2, and A and B are mutually exclusive

questions.question: Bag I contains 3 red and 2 black balls; Bag II contains 2 red and 3 black balls. A bag is chosen at random and a ball drawn from it is red. What is the probability that it came from Bag I?

cu-mangrove.title: Factual passage: Mangroves
cu-mangrove.html:
Factual passage: Mangroves

Along many tropical coasts, where rivers meet the sea, grow forests that seem to stand on stilts. These are mangroves, trees and shrubs that can survive in salty, waterlogged mud that would kill most other plants. Some mangroves filter much of the salt out at their roots; others get rid of it through their leaves. Because the mud holds very little oxygen, several species send up pencil-like roots from the ground. These breathing roots, called pneumatophores, take in air at low tide.

Mangroves matter far beyond the narrow strip they occupy. Their tangled roots slow down waves and trap sediment, so they help protect the shore from erosion and reduce the damage done by storm surges. The calm, shaded water between the roots is a nursery for young fish, crabs and prawns, many of which later move out to the open sea, where they support coastal fishing. Mangrove soils also store large amounts of carbon that would otherwise add to the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

Despite these benefits, mangroves have been cleared in many places for fish farms, ports and housing. Once removed, they are slow to return, because seedlings need sheltered mud and the right mix of fresh and salt water to take root. Restoration projects tend to succeed when local communities, who depend on the forest for fish and firewood, are involved in planting and protecting it. Without such involvement, newly planted areas are often lost again within a few years.

cu-radio.title: Narrative passage: The radio
cu-radio.html:
Narrative passage: The radio

The radio had been silent for eleven years when Meera carried it down from the loft. It was a heavy wooden box with a cracked dial and a smell of dust and old varnish. Her grandfather watched from his chair as she set it on the table.

"It won't work," he said. "Nothing in it has worked since your grandmother passed away."

Meera said nothing. She had spent the summer helping at her uncle's repair shop, and she had learned that most broken things were not as broken as people believed. She unscrewed the back panel. Inside, among the glass valves and coloured wires, she found what she had half expected: a wire that had come loose from its terminal, its end green with corrosion.

It took her most of the afternoon. She cleaned the terminal, cut back the wire and borrowed her uncle's soldering iron. Her grandfather pretended to read the newspaper, but she noticed that he had not turned a page in an hour.

When she finally switched it on, there was only a low hum. Then, slowly, as the valves warmed, a voice rose out of the static, reading the evening news in the same calm tone the old man must have heard a thousand times.

He put down the newspaper. For a long moment he did not speak. Then he reached over and turned the dial, very carefully, to a station that played old film songs.

"She liked this one," he said quietly, and Meera understood that she had repaired more than a radio.

cu-monsoon.title: Literary passage: The first rain
cu-monsoon.html:
Literary passage: The first rain

The first rain of the monsoon does not arrive so much as announce itself. For days the sky has been a sheet of tin, the air thick enough to lean on, and the city has waited with the irritable patience of a queue that has stopped moving. Then the wind changes. Leaves turn their pale undersides to the sky, as if to check what is coming, and somewhere a door bangs shut.

When the drops come, they are large and few, each one landing on the dusty road with a sound like a coin dropped on a table. Children run out before their mothers can stop them. Shopkeepers, who have spent the week complaining of the heat, stand in their doorways and complain instead about the mud, though their faces say otherwise.

And then there is the smell. The parched earth, touched by water, releases a scent so particular that we have borrowed a scientist's word, petrichor, to name it, though no word quite contains it. For a moment the whole city seems to breathe out.

By evening the gutters are rivers and the traffic has given up. Tomorrow there will be potholes, leaking roofs and the long grey weeks of the season. But tonight nobody is thinking of tomorrow. Tonight the rain is not weather; it is a reprieve.
